compound-interest-calculator.assumptionNote: Assumes a constant rate, contributions added at the end of each compounding period, and no withdrawals, fees, or tax.
benefits: Makes the abstract idea of compounding concrete and personal.
Shows exactly how much each extra year of patience is worth.
Lets you compare bank, bond, and fund offers on equal terms.
Motivates starting early — the growth curve does the convincing.

faqs.a: It is interest on interest. In year one you earn interest on your deposit; in year two you earn interest on your deposit plus last year's interest. Each cycle the base grows, so growth accelerates — slowly at first, then dramatically.
faqs.q: What is compound interest in simple words?

faqs.a: Simple interest pays only on the original principal every year, so growth is a straight line. Compound interest reinvests each year's interest, so growth curves upward. Over 10 years at 8%, ₹50,000 earns ₹40,000 simple but ₹60,982 compounded monthly.
faqs.q: How is it different from simple interest?

faqs.a: A little. Daily compounding beats annual compounding, but on a 10-year investment the gap is usually under 1% of the final amount. Rate and time dominate — do not pick an investment for its compounding frequency alone.

Divide 72 by your annual rate to estimate doubling time. At 8%, money doubles in about 9 years (72/8). It is a handy mental check on this calculator's results — our example nearly doubles in 10 years, which matches.

Because each contribution gets the full remaining time to compound. ₹5,000 a month at 10% for 20 years becomes about ₹38 lakh, of which only ₹12 lakh was your own money — the rest is growth doing the heavy lifting.
faqs.q: Why do small contributions matter so much?

faqs.a: Yes — on debt. Credit card balances compound monthly against you at 36–42% APR, which is why minimum payments barely move the balance. Compounding is a tool: on investments it builds wealth, on debt it builds the lender's wealth.

compound-interest-calculator.formula: A = P x (1 + r/n)^(n x t) + PMT x (((1 + r/n)^(n x t) - 1) / (r/n)), where P = principal, r = annual rate, n = compounding frequency, t = years, PMT = contribution per period.
howTo: Set the years and any monthly contribution, then read the final amount.
keyFacts: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest, not just on your principal.
Time matters more than rate: starting 10 years earlier beats a 2% higher rate started late.
More frequent compounding helps, but the effect is small next to rate and time.
Regular contributions supercharge compounding because each deposit gets its own growth runway.
Inflation is the silent opponent — an 8% return at 6% inflation is only about 2% real growth.

Shows nominal growth; inflation-adjusted (real) growth will be lower.

compound-interest-calculator.quickAnswer: ₹50,000 invested at 8% per year, compounded monthly for 10 years, grows to ₹110,982 — earning ₹60,982 in interest, more than the original deposit. That extra comes from interest earning its own interest, and it accelerates the longer you stay invested.
compound-interest-calculator.tagline: Watch your money grow with compounding — final amount, interest earned, and the true power of time.
compound-interest-calculator.workedExample:
Principal ₹50,000, 8% annual rate, monthly compounding (n = 12), 10 years, no extra contributions:
1. Monthly rate = 0.08 / 12 = 0.0066667.
2. Periods = 12 x 10 = 120.
3. Growth factor = (1.0066667)^120 = 2.21964.
4. Final = 50,000 x 2.21964 = ₹110,982.01.
5. Interest = 110,982.01 - 50,000 = ₹60,982.01 — more than the starting amount.
